title: Probability Distributions and Expected Value
seo_title: Expected Value Worksheet: Probability Distributions, Games, Binomial | 100 Questions
standard_text: Calculate the expected value of a random variable; interpret it as the mean of the probability distribution.
meta_desc: Free precalculus worksheet on probability distributions and expected value: tables, games, fair games, binomial probabilities, insurance and warranties. 100 questions.
key_big: E(X) = Σ x · P(x), the long-run average.
key_sub: Use net gain for games; a fair game has E(X) = 0.
body_html:
How it works

  • A probability distribution lists each value of X with its probability. Every probability is from 0 to 1, and they add to 1.
  • Expected value: E(X) = Σ x · P(x), the long-run average.
  • For a game, use the net gain (prize minus cost). A game is fair when the expected net gain is 0.
  • Binomial: in n independent trials with success probability p, P(X = k) = nCk pk(1 − p)n−k and E(X) = np.
  • To decide between options, compare expected values (or expected costs).
Example

A game costs $2. You win $10 with probability 0.15. Find the expected net gain.

Expected prize = 10 × 0.15 = $1.50

$1.50 − $2

Answer: −$0.50

Example

A seed sprouts with probability 0.8. Find P(exactly 3 of 4 sprout).

4C3(0.8)³(0.2)¹

= 4 × 0.512 × 0.2

Answer: 0.4096

Common mistakes

  • Averaging the values without using the probabilities.
  • Forgetting to subtract the cost to play.
  • Leaving out nCk in a binomial probability.
  • Choosing an option by the size of the prize alone.

faq.q: How do you calculate expected value?
faq.a: Multiply each outcome by its probability and add the products: E(X) = Σ x · P(x).
A game whose expected net gain is 0, so on average you neither win nor lose money.

faq.q: What is the expected value of a binomial distribution?
faq.a: E(X) = np, where n is the number of trials and p is the probability of success.

faq.q: How is expected value used to make decisions?
faq.a: Compare the expected gain or cost of each choice, such as a warranty price against the expected cost of repairs.

A spinner pays $8, $2 or $0 with probabilities 0.2, 0.2 and 0.6. It costs $2 to spin. What is the expected net gain per spin?
items.e: Expected prize = 8(0.2) + 2(0.2) + 0(0.6) = $2. Subtract the cost: $2 − $2 = $0.

items.q: A game costs $2 to play. You roll a number cube and win $9 if you roll a 6; otherwise you win nothing. What is the expected value of your net gain?
items.e: Expected prize = $9 × 1/6 = $1.50. Subtract the cost to play: $1.50 − $2 = −$0.50.
